title: Text as a feature
objectives: Build a daily text feature stamped with when each document became known.

screens.title: What was known at the close?
screens.prose: A desk turns news into a daily feature. Each document has a publication time and a sentiment score. Positions are set at the 16:30 close each day, so a document helps a decision only if it was out by then.
screens.question: What is the mean score of the documents published after Monday's close and by Tuesday's? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Which documents fall between Monday 16:30 and Tuesday 16:30?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use publication times against the 16:30 close.

byKey.two: You dropped d2. It came out at 16:35 on Monday, after that day's close, so it first feeds Tuesday.

explain.text: A document belongs to the first close at or after its publication: d2 feeds Tuesday, d5 feeds Wednesday. Tuesday's mean is 0.1333.

screens.title: The as-of join
screens.prose: The simplest feature is the latest score known at each day's close. That is `fin-ml` level 2's **as-of join**: for each decision time, take the last document at or before it, `pd.merge_asof(days, docs, direction='backward')`.
screens.question: What is the as-of feature for Wednesday 8 March?

hints.text: The last document at or before Wed 16:30.

feedback.correct: d7's 0.1: the last document out before the close.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the latest document at or before Wednesday 16:30.

byKey.forward: −0.2 is d8, published Thursday morning: a forward join, which looks into the future.
byKey.first: 0.5 is d6, Wednesday's first document; d7 came later, before the close.

explain.text: Backward means the most recent past document, here d7's 0.1. A forward join would hand Wednesday d8 from Thursday, a value nobody had at the time.

options.text: Monday's close, since it is the same day
options.why: Positions were set at 16:30; d2 did not exist then.

options.text: Tuesday's open, if the desk trades at the open
options.why: This desk sets positions only at the close.
Dropping them throws away news; they feed the next close.

hints.text: Positions are set at 16:30 each day.

feedback.correct: Tuesday's close, the first decision after it appeared.
feedback.generic: Not quite. When is the next decision after Monday 16:35?

explain.text: An after-close document belongs to the next decision. Dating it to its calendar day hands Monday's close information from after it.

screens.title: Several documents a day
screens.prose: Most days have several documents. A daily feature can take their mean score and also their count, which says how much news there was.
screens.question: For Wednesday's close, what is the mean score of the documents published since Tuesday's close? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Include every document between the two closes.

byKey.by-date: You took Wednesday's documents by date. d5 came out after Tuesday's close, so it belongs here too.

explain.text: Mean 0.10 from three documents. Keeping the count beside the mean lets a model trust a day with ten documents more than a day with one.

screens.title: Older news counts less
screens.prose: Instead of a window, weight every known document by its age: with a **half-life** of $h$ days, a document $a$ days old gets weight $0.5^{a/h}$, and the feature is the weighted mean score. At Wednesday's close, d1 is 2.3021 days old.
screens.question: With a half-life of 1 day, what weight does d1 get? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Raise 0.5 to the age in half-lives.

byKey.whole-days: You rounded the age to 2 whole days. d1 is 2 days and 7 hours old: 2.3021 days.

explain.text: d1 is $2 + 7.25/24 = 2.3021$ days old, so it keeps $0.2028$ of its weight. Over all seven known documents the decayed score at Wednesday's close is 0.2032.

screens.title: Event date or publication date
screens.prose: Corran's results for the quarter ending 30 September were published on 8 November. A dataset stamps each results document with the quarter end, the date the numbers describe.
screens.question: By how many calendar days does that stamp put the document too early?

hints.text: Count the days left in September, then October, then November.

feedback.correct: 39 days: a backtest would trade on the results five and a half weeks before anyone saw them.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count from 30 September to 8 November.

byKey.zero: You treated the quarter end as the date it was known. The numbers describe 30 September but were published on 8 November.
byKey.months: 31 is October alone; add the 8 days of November.

explain.text: From 30 September to 8 November is 39 days. A text feature is dated by when it became known, never by the period it describes.

screens.title: A day with no news
screens.prose: Friday 10 March has no new document. The last one known is d8, from Thursday morning.
screens.question: Which treatment of Friday is honest?

options.text: Carry d8 forward with its age, or leave Friday missing

options.why: 0 claims neutral news was published; there was none at all.

options.text: Use the first document of the following week
options.why: That document did not exist on Friday: it is look-ahead.
Dropping no-news days quietly changes the trading calendar and biases the test.

hints.text: Which choices use only what was known on Friday?

feedback.correct: Carry forward with an age column, or leave it missing; both are honest if stated.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which treatments use only past information?

explain.text: Carrying forward uses only the past; the age column lets a model discount stale news. Leaving it missing is honest too, if the model handles gaps.

screens.title: A feature stamped when known
screens.prose:
What you did: assign each document to the first decision time at or after its publication, then aggregate per day,

$$x_t = \frac{\sum_{i : p_i \le \tau_t} w_i s_i}{\sum_{i : p_i \le \tau_t} w_i}, \qquad w_i = 0.5^{(\tau_t - p_i)/h},$$

with $p_i$ the publication time, $\tau_t$ the decision time on day $t$ and $h$ the half-life.
screens.question: Which join builds this feature without look-ahead?

options.text: An as-of join on publication time, direction backward

options.why: Forward takes the next document after the decision: the future.

options.text: An exact join on the calendar date
options.why: It ignores the time, so after-close documents leak into the same day.

options.text: A join on the event date the text describes
options.why: The event date can be weeks before publication.

hints.text: Each decision may use the latest document before it.

feedback.correct: Backward as-of join on publication time.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which join only looks into the past?

explain.text: A backward as-of join on publication time gives each decision the documents out before it, and nothing later.

widget.solution:
import datetime as dt


def decayed_score(docs, day, half_life, decision_time='16:30'):
    t = dt.datetime.fromisoformat(day + ' ' + decision_time)
    num = den = 0.0
    for d in docs:
        p = dt.datetime.fromisoformat(d['published'])
        if p > t:
            continue
        w = 0.5 ** ((t - p).total_seconds() / 86400 / half_life)
        num += w * d['score']
        den += w
    return num / den if den > 0 else None
widget.how: Submit runs 7 hidden tests within relative $10^{-9}$ (the long half-life within $10^{-6}$). They cover two documents exactly 1 and 2 days old, Friday with a 2-day half-life, and Wednesday with 1 day and 1,000 days (nearly a plain mean). Then Monday with half a day, a day before any document, and a 09:00 decision time.

screens.title: Tone of an earnings call
screens.prose: A desk scores the tone of earnings-call transcripts for 400 shares. A call held at 14:00 is transcribed and published by the vendor at 21:30 the same day, after the 16:30 close.
screens.question: Which day's decision should the call's tone feed?

options.text: The next day's close, as the transcript was published after today's
The same day's close, since the call was at 14:00
options.why: Your feed had no text at 14:00; the transcript arrived at 21:30.

options.text: Whenever the call happened, since tone is fixed then
options.why: The tone existed at 14:00, but your data did not.

options.text: A week later, to be safe
options.why: That throws away a real edge for no reason; the next close is enough.

hints.text: Which timestamp does your data carry: the call's or the publication's?

feedback.correct: The next close: the feature is stamped when your data had it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. When did your feed have the transcript?

explain.text: Stamp by the vendor's publication time, 21:30, so the tone feeds the next close. Listening live would change that, but only if the desk really did.

ideas: A document feeds the first decision at or after its publication time; one published after the close belongs to the next day.
Build daily features with a backward as-of join on publication time: the latest score, a mean and count since the last close, or a decayed mean.
Date text by when it became known, never by the period it describes, and say how no-news days are treated.
